'''Holnicote''' {{IPAc-en|ˈ|h|ʌ|n|ɪ|ˌ|k|ʌ|t}} (pronounced "Hunnicutt") in the parish of [[Selworthy]], West [[Somerset]], England, is a historic [[Estate in land|estate]] consisting of 12,420 acres (5,026 hectares) of land, much situated within the [[Exmoor|Exmoor National Park]].

There have been several houses on the estate over the last 500 years. In 1705 a new mansion was built which was burned down in 1779. It was rebuilt as a hunting lodge and survived until another fire in 1851 and replaced ten years later. It became one of the centres for the [[Devon and Somerset Staghounds]]. The main building was damaged by another fire in 1941. The house and surrounding estate were given to the [[National Trust]] in 1944 by [[Richard Acland|Sir Richard Thomas Dyke Acland, 15th Baronet]]. The house is now operated as an hotel. The surrounding land which includes [[Dunkery Hill|Dunkery]] and [[Selworthy Beacon]]s, and the villages and hamlets of Selworthy, [[Allerford]], [[Bossington (Somerset)|Bossington]], [[Horner, Somerset|Horner]] and [[Luccombe, Somerset|Luccombe]] as well as the Dunkery and Horner Woods [[List of national nature reserves in Somerset|National Nature Reserve]] contains more than {{convert|240|km|-1}} of [[Trail|footpaths]] and bridleways.

In the 13th and 14th centuries the estate was held by the de Holne family. During the 17th century the Staynings were [[Lord of the manor|lords of the manor]] and in the 18th descendants of [[FitzMartin]] by then known as the Martyn family had taken over. William Martin sold Holnicote to William Blackford and it descended through his family and then passed to the Dyke family. Sir Thomas Acland married into the family and added the surname to become [[Sir Thomas Dyke Acland, 7th Baronet]] and it remained in his family until the donation in 1944.

==History==
{{main|Descent of Holnicote}}

===Early===
[[File:HolnicoteDomesdayBook.png|thumb|The [[Domesday Book]] entry for ''Honecote'', showing the manor held by two nuns]]

Alternative derivations of the name Holnicote, which was spelled variously as ''Honecote,'' ''Hunecote'' or ''Hunecota'', have been suggested.{{sfn|Chadwyck-Healey|1901|p=6}} It may relate to ''holegn'', the [[Old English|Anglo-Saxon]] word for holly.<ref>{{cite web|first1=John |last1=Fisher |url=http://www.dartmoor.gov.uk/__data/assets/pdf_file/0006/127158/Selworthy.pdf |title=Selworthy: Conservation Area Character Appraisal, 2004 |publisher=Exmoor National Park Authority |access-date=21 May 2015 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150523014819/http://www.dartmoor.gov.uk/__data/assets/pdf_file/0006/127158/Selworthy.pdf |archive-date=23 May 2015 }}</ref> [[Eilert Ekwall]] supports the claim that places which start ''Holne'' come from the Old English ''holegn'' meaning holly,{{sfn|Ekwall|1960|p=247}} while Stephen Robinson, in his book on local place names prefers an explanation "The Honey Cottage" from the Old English ''honeg'' and ''cot''.{{sfn|Robinson|1992|p=77}} In the 19th century, the Rector of Selworthy, the Rev. F. Hancock, who was said to have extensively studied the place-names of his parish, preferred the old English personal name ''Hùn'' for the first element.<ref>{{cite book
|title=An Exploration of Exmoor and the Hill Country of West Somerset: With Notes on Its Archaeology
|author=Page, John Lloyd Warden
|year=1895|page=162
|publisher=Seeley & Co. Ltd}}</ref>

There are several references in the [[Domesday Book]] to ''Honecote'', ''Hunnecota'' or ''Hunecota'' in the [[Hundred (county division)|hundred]] of [[Hundred of Carhampton|Carhampton]]. One records land held by one William of the [[tenant-in-chief]], Roger de Corcelle; prior to the [[Norman conquest of England|Norman Conquest]], this land belonged to two theigns called Aluric and Bristeuin. Odo, son of Gamelin, held a detached portion of this land. The second record shows two nuns holding two and half [[virgate]]s.{{refn|group=nb|Chadwyck-Healey provides a translation of the Domesday materials and in his index, he identifies the passages as referring to Holnicote. The extracts are from pages 179 (referring to the nuns), 403 (referring to de Corcelle) and 475 (referring to Odo) of the Exon Domesday Book, and folios 91d (referring to the nuns) and 94 (referring to de Corcelle) from the Great Domesday Book.{{sfn|Chadwyck-Healey|1901|p = 6}}}} The local historian and lawyer [[Charles Chadwyck-Healey]] identifies these manors with modern Holnicote,{{sfn|Chadwyck-Healey|1901|p = 6}} the National Archives agrees with him in their catalogue,{{refn|group="nb"|The catalogue entries for the Great Domesday Book are at {{cite web|title=Place name: Holnicote, Somerset|url=http://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/D7302676|publisher=National Archives|access-date=20 May 2015}} and {{Cite web|url=http://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/D7302509 |title=Place name: Holnicote Somerset |publisher=National Archives |access-date=4 June 2015}} They refer to folios 94 recto and 91 verso respectively, which equate to the entries for de Corcelle and the nuns (cf. {{Harvnb|Chadwyck-Healey|1901|p = 6}}).}} and the Open Domesday project lists them under Holnicote,<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://opendomesday.org/place/SS9046/holnicote/ |title=Place: Holnicote |publisher=Open Domesday |access-date=4 June 2015}}</ref> but the editors of the ''[[Victoria County History]]'' series only identify the land held by the nuns with Holnicote and state that de Corcelle's manor was actually Huntscott in Wootton Courtney.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/som/vol1/pp479-526 |title=''Text of the Somerset Domesday: Part 2 A History of the County of Somerset'', vol. 1|first1= William |last1=Page |date=1906|website=British History Online|publisher=Victoria County History|access-date=22 May 2015}}</ref>

There is scarce evidence regarding the holders of Holnicote in the period immediately after Domesday. William de Holne held the manor in the reign of [[Edward I of England|Edward I]]. Although Chadwyck-Healey described it is "very probable" that this William de Holne is the same man recorded elsewhere with a son, Richard, whose daughter Thomasia married John, son of Walter Gofreye, the evidence is not conclusive. {{sfn|Chadwyck-Healey|1901|p = 191}} By the late 15th century, the Steynings family were claiming descent from the Huish and de Holne dynasties. Their origins are obscure and the earliest record of them is the will of William Steynings, which was proved in 1491. His son, Edward, died in 1524/5 and was succeeded by his son Walter; Edward Steynings's will refers to property at Holnicote. Eventually, his grandson Thomas became owner of the manor and house of Holnicote; he is listed in Crown account books as early as 1558. His younger brother, Philip (died 1588/9), succeeded him at Holnicote.{{sfn|Chadwyck-Healey|1901|pp = 193-196}}
[[File:All Saints church, Selworthy - monument to Charles Staynings.jpg|thumb|upright|Memorial tablet to Charles Staynings (died 1700) in [[Church of All Saints, Selworthy]]]]

===Martyn and Blackford families===
The Steynings family owned Holnicote until the direct male line became extinct with the death of Charles Staynings (1622–1700). His wife, Susanna (died 1685), was a daughter of Sir [[Nicholas Martyn]] of Oxton and Steynings's heir was their nephew, William Martyn.<ref>Rev. F. Hancock, "The Ancient Chapel in the Parish of Holnicote", ''Proceedings of the Somersetshire Archaeological and Natural History Society'', vol. 39 (1893), pp. 55–56: "The principal landowners in the parish of seem, however, to have been from time immemorial to the death of the last direct representative of the family in 1701, the of was purchased from Mr. nephew,  Martin, of in South Devon, by Richard Blackford, of This family held it for two generations, and then on the death of its Infant heiress it reverted to her aunt, Elizabeth Dyke, of Pixton who brought it as her dower to the Sir Thomas Acland of the day."</ref>{{sfn|Hancock|1897|p = 55}} According to records of the Heralds' Visitations of Devon and research by the Victorian historian [[John Lambrick Vivian]], this William Martyn lived in Oxton in the parish of [[Kenton, Devon]]; he was Susanna Martyn's great-nephew and died in 1710, aged 30.{{sfn|Vivian|1895|p = 554}}<ref>P. F. S. Amery, John S. Amery and J. Brooking Rowe (eds.), ''[[iarchive:devoncornwallno01unkngoog|Devon Notes and Queries]]'', vol. ii (1903), p. 65</ref> He sold the estate to William Blackford, a [[Court of Chancery|Master in Chancery]].<ref name=":0">F. Hancock, "Notes on the Parish of Selworthy. 1—The Church" in Frederic William Weaver and Charles Herbert Mayo (eds.), ''Notes and Queries for Somerset and Dorset'', vol. 3 (1893), pp. 330–331</ref> Blackford then bought the manors of [[Bossington, Somerset|Bossington]] and Avill, the latter from Anthony Stocker and his wife, Sarah; this estate extended from the ridge of Grabbist nearly to the sea-shore and also included land in the parishes of Dunster, Carhampton, Crowcombe, Stogumber, Timberscombe and St. Decumans.{{sfn|Maxwell Lyte|1909|p = 442}} He married Elizabeth, a daughter of John Dyke of [[Pixton Park|Pixton]], and died in 1728.<ref name=":0" /> His son, William, succeeded him and married Henrietta Collet (died 1727), a daughter and co-heiress of Joseph Collet of [[Hertford Castle]] in Hertfordshire.{{sfn|Hancock|1897|pp = 171–175}} However, he died only three years after his father. Their only daughter and heiress, Henrietta Blackford, inherited the estate as an infant, but died aged 7 in 1733.<ref name=":0" />{{sfn|Maxwell Lyte|1909|p = 442}} The estates were divisible upon a great-aunt, Elizabeth Dyke (died 1737), and a second cousin, Elizabeth, a daughter of Thomas Dyke of Tetton and Mary, a daughter of Elizabeth Dyke (died 1737). Later in 1733, Elizabeth Dyke (died 1737) conveyed her share in the estate to her only surviving son, Edward Dyke (died 1746) who in turn conveyed his portion to his niece in 1744, making her the sole owner of the entire estate.{{sfn|Maxwell Lyte|1909|p = 442}}<ref>Chadwyck-Healey, pp. 316-318. The great aunt, Elizabeth Dyke, was a daughter of Richard Blackford, the father of William Blackford, who bought the Holnicote estate from William Martyn. Richard Blackford's only other known child was a daughter, Sidwell, who married Thomas Dyke; their son, Thomas, had a daughter, Elizabeth, the other co-heiress of the Blackford estates.</ref>[[File:SirThomasDykeAcland7thBtByReynolds.jpg|thumb|upright|[[Sir Thomas Dyke Acland, 7th Baronet]] (1723–1785). Portrait, 1767, by Sir [[Joshua Reynolds]], on display at [[Killerton]] House.<ref>{{cite web|title=Sir Thomas Dyke Acland (1722–1785), 7th Bt, MP|url=https://artuk.org/discover/artworks/sir-thomas-dyke-acland-17221785-7th-bt-mp-100361|website=[[Art UK]]|access-date=23 May 2015}}</ref> A similar painting, which is also owned by the [[National Trust]] can be seen at [[Saltram House]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Sir Thomas Dyke Acland (1722–1785), 3rd Bt, MP|url=https://artuk.org/discover/artworks/sir-thomas-dyke-acland-17221785-3rd-bt-mp-101578|website=[[Art UK]]}}</ref>|left]]

===Acland family===
Elizabeth Dyke married [[Sir Thomas Dyke Acland, 7th Baronet]] (1722–1785) of Killerton in Devon and [[Petherton Park]] in Somerset in 1745.{{sfn|Maxwell Lyte|1909|p = 442}}{{sfn|Richardson|1996|p = 73}} A prominent member of the [[West Country]] gentry, Acland was a famous [[Devon and Somerset Staghounds|staghunter]] who used his wife's [[Exmoor]] estates of Holnicote and Pixton as his hunting seats.{{sfn|Lauder|2002|pp = 226-231}} He built kennels for the North Devon Staghounds{{sfn|Lauder|2002|pp = 226-231}} and kept his own pack of dogs.{{sfn|Lysons|Lysons|1822|pp = 226-231}} He became forester or ranger of Exmoor under grant from [[the Crown]], a title for the king's chief officer of the [[royal forest]]. According to the [[Victorian era|Victorian]] author, Charles Palk Collyns, he "hunted the country in almost princely style. Respected and beloved by all the countryside, he was solicited at the same time to allow himself to be returned as member of [[Parliament of Great Britain|Parliament]] for the counties of Devon and Somerset. He preferred, however, the duties and pleasures of life in the country, where he bore without abuse the grand old name of gentleman".{{sfn|Collyns|1862|p=9}} Although he had three of his own kennels, he had a further method of keeping hounds at Holnicote, Jury and Highercombe, whereby he made the keeping of one hound a term a stipulation of many of the tenancies he granted. In his manor of Bossington (near Holnicote) alone an estate survey of 1746–1747 lists twelve [[Tenement (law)|tenements]] let, either by Acland or Dyke, with the requirement to keep a hound.{{sfn|Ravenhill|Rowe|2006|p = 8}}

In 1775 he handed over the mastership to the then Major Basset, and in 1779 his beloved collection of stag heads and antlers at Holnicote was lost in a fire which also destroyed the house. He declared that "he minded the destruction of his valuables less bitterly than the loss of his fine collection of stags' heads".{{sfn|Acland|1981|p = 25}} He was known on his estates as "Sir Thomas his Honour"{{sfn|Acland|1981|p = 26}} (as later was his son the 9th Baronet) and was renowned for his generous hospitality at Holnicote or at Pixton, whichever was closest, to all riders "in at the death",{{sfn|Acland|1981|p = 18}} and it is said that by the architect Anne Acland that "open house was kept at Pixton and Holnicote throughout the hunting season".<ref>Acland, 1981, p.19</ref>

Acland's eldest son died as a result of wounds aged 34. His grandson died at the age of 7 a few weeks after inheriting the baronetcy and so his second son, [[Sir Thomas Dyke Acland, 9th Baronet|Thomas Dyke Acland]] (1752–1794), became the ninth Baronet. Like his father, he was known locally in Devon and Somerset as "Sir Thomas his Honour"{{sfn|Acland|1981|p = 26}} and they shared a passion for stag hunting. He followed him into the Mastership of the North Devon Staghounds and virtually abandoned the family's main [[English country house|seat]] of Killerton in mid-Devon to live at Holnicote and Highercombe, near [[Dulverton]], on the north and south edges respectively of the ancient royal forest of Exmoor, renown for its herds of [[red deer]]. During the period 1785 to his death in 1794 he killed 101 stags, the heads and antlers of many of which are still displayed in the stables at Holnicote.{{sfn|Acland|1981|pp = 25-26}} He was a stern employer of his hunt-staff, and on one occasion when his hounds had killed several sheep, possibly belonging to his farming tenants, he ordered his huntsman "to hang himself and the whole pack".{{sfn|Acland|1981|p = 27}}

The estate passed down through the Acland family<ref>{{cite web|last=Richardson|first=I.J.|title=The Acland Family and Exmoor|url=http://www.exmoorher.co.uk/hbsmr-web/record.aspx?UID=TEM34-The-Acland-Family-and-Exmoor-(Thematic-Essay)|publisher=Exmoor National Park|website=Exmoor Historic Environment Record|access-date=15 December 2013|archive-date=15 December 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131215171801/http://www.exmoorher.co.uk/hbsmr-web/record.aspx?UID=TEM34-The-Acland-Family-and-Exmoor-(Thematic-Essay)|url-status=dead}}</ref> until February 1944, when Sir Richard Dyke Acland, 15th Baronet (1906–1990) donated the Holnicote and Killerton Estates to the National Trust, comprising {{convert|16000|acre}}, which was the largest ever donation received by the National Trust.<ref>{{cite news|title=Killerton and Holnicote Handed Over to National Trust|url=http://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0000265/19440204/042/0006|access-date=19 October 2014|work=Western Times|date=4 February 1944| via = [[British Newspaper Archive]]|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Estate==
[[File:Holnicote 1785 ByFrancisTowne.jpg|thumb|left|Holnicote House in 1785, as rebuilt after the fire of 1779, viewed from the south-west. In the foreground is [[Sir Thomas Dyke Acland, 9th Baronet]], with staghounds. Oil painting, 1785, by [[Francis Towne]], in the National Trust collection at Killerton House.]]
The estate had a role, together with the Acland family's other Exmoor estate of Pixton, as a home of West Country staghunting in the 18th century.{{sfn|Acland|1981|pp=15–28}} There was some controversy locally and nationally when the National Trust banned stag hunting on the estate in the early 21st century.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Rowe|first1=Mark |title=Trust defeats hunt lobby on stag ban|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/trust-defeats-hunt-lobby-on-stag-ban-1183467.html |access-date=23 May 2015|work=Independent|date=8 November 1998}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Rowe|first1=Mark |title=Trust defeats hunt lobby on stag ban|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/trust-defeats-hunt-lobby-on-stag-ban-1183467.html |access-date=21 January 2015|work=Independent|date=8 November 1998}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Parker|first1=Simon |title=National Trust hits back at Lords attack|url=https://www.theguardian.com/society/2001/nov/13/charitymanagement |access-date=21 January 2015|work=Guardian|date=13 November 2001}}</ref><ref>{{cite hansard |jurisdiction=House of Commons |title=National Trust |url=https://api.parliament.uk/historic-hansard/lords/2001/nov/12/national-trust |date=12 November 2001 |column_start=424 |column_end=428 |speaker=Lord Patten }}</ref>

Holnicote Estate covers more than {{convert|12,000|acre}} and contains more than {{convert|240|km|-1}} of [[Trail|footpaths]] and [[Bridle path|bridleways]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Holnicote Estate|url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/holnicote-estate/ |publisher=National Trust|access-date=19 October 2014}}</ref> It includes [[Dunkery Hill|Dunkery]] and [[Selworthy Beacon]]s,<ref>{{cite news|title=Holnicote Estate, Somerset: walk of the week|url= https://www.telegraph.co.uk/travel/activityandadventure/walkingholidays/8252663/Holnicote-Estate-Somerset-walk-of-the-week.html |access-date=23 May 2015|work=Telegraph|date=12 January 2011}}</ref> and the villages and hamlets of Selworthy, Allerford, [[Bossington (Somerset)|Bossington]], [[Horner, Somerset|Horner]] and [[Luccombe, Somerset|Luccombe]] as well as the Dunkery and Horner Woods [[National nature reserves in Somerset|National Nature Reserve]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Somerset's National Nature Reserves|url=https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/somersets-national-nature-reserves |publisher=UK Government|access-date=21 January 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Dunkery and Horner Wood NNR|url= http://www.naturalengland.org.uk/ourwork/conservation/designatedareas/nnr/1006951.aspx |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20090206103524/http://www.naturalengland.org.uk/ourwork/conservation/designatedareas/nnr/1006951.aspx |url-status=dead|archive-date=6 February 2009|publisher=Natural England|access-date=21 January 2015}}</ref> The estate also plays host to a [[Point-to-point (steeplechase)|point to point]] course on which many Exmoor hunts hold their meetings throughout the spring.<ref>{{cite web|title=Holnicote, Somerset |url=http://www.pointtopoint.co.uk/go/courses/holnicote.html |publisher=Point-To-Point |access-date=23 May 2015 |url-status=dead |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20150319071118/http://pointtopoint.co.uk/go/courses/holnicote.html |archive-date=19 March 2015 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Holnicote Point-to-Point |url=http://www.thebestofexmoor.co.uk/whats-on-on-exmoor/holnicote-point-to-points |publisher=The Best of Exmoor |access-date=19 October 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20141019125105/http://www.thebestofexmoor.co.uk/whats-on-on-exmoor/holnicote-point-to-points |archive-date=19 October 2014 }}</ref>

Dunkery Beacon is the summit of Dunkery Hill, and the highest point on Exmoor and in Somerset. The [[sandstone]] hill rises to {{convert|1705|ft|m|0}} and provides views over the surrounding moorland, the [[Bristol Channel]] and hills up to {{convert|86|mi|km|0}} away. The site has been visited by humans since the [[Bronze Age]] with several [[Tumulus|burial mounds]] in the form of [[cairn]]s and [[bowl barrow]]s.<ref>{{National Heritage List for England of cairns, thought to be the remains of [[round barrow]]s,{{sfn|Adkins|Adkins|1992|p=101}} and the Iron Age [[Bury Castle, Somerset|Bury Castle]].{{sfn|Dunning|1980|p=125}} The round cairns have been some unique [[whitebeam]] species. [[Exmoor pony|Exmoor ponies]], red deer, [[European pied flycatcher|pied flycatcher]]s, [[wood warbler]]s, [[lesser spotted woodpecker]]s, [[Common redstart|redstarts]], [[white-throated dipper|dippers]], [[Common snipe|snipe]], [[Alauda|skylarks]] and [[Common kestrel|kestrels]] are some of the fauna to be found here and in nearby Horner Woods. Horner Woods are also the home to 14 of the 16 UK [[bat]] species, which include [[barbastelle]] and [[Bechstein's bat]]s.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Riley|first1=Hazel |last2=Wilson-North|first2=Robert |title=The Field Archaeology of Exmoor|url= http://archaeologydataservice.ac.uk/archiveDS/archiveDownload?t=arch-1416-1/dissemination/pdf/9781848021495_all.pdf |publisher=Archaeology Data Service|access-date=24 January 2015}}</ref>
[[File:HolnicoteStables Selworthy Somerset.JPG|thumb|Stalls in stable block built by Sir Thomas Dyke Acland, 9th Baronet (1752–1794) at Holnicote. The 30 stag heads on the walls date from about 1787 to 1793 and were killed under his mastership of the [[Devon and Somerset Staghounds]].{{sfn|Acland|1981|p=25}}]]
Selworthy is a small village and [[Civil parishes in England|civil parish]] which includes the [[Hamlet (place)|hamlets]] of Bossington, Tivington, Lynch, Brandish Street and Allerford. Bossington is separated from [[Porlock Bay]] by a shingle beach, through which flows the [[River Horner]], forming part of the [[Porlock Ridge and Saltmarsh]] [[Site of Special Scientific Interest]]. In the 1990s rising sea levels created salt marshes, and lagoons developed in the area behind the boulder bank.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-coastal-issues.pdf |title=Shifting shores in the South West |publisher=National Trust |access-date=13 October 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20081206034626/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-coastal-issues.pdf |archive-date= 6 December 2008 }}</ref> The village is on the South West Coast Path. Selworthy was rebuilt as a [[model village]], to provide housing for the aged and infirm of the Holnicote estate, in 1828 by Sir Thomas Acland.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.touruk.co.uk/houses/housesomer_selworthy.htm |title=Selworthy |access-date=26 January 2008 |work=Tour UK |url-status=dead |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20080113010841/http://www.touruk.co.uk/houses/housesomer_selworthy.htm |archive-date=13 January 2008 }}</ref> Many of the other cottages, some of which are now rented out, are still [[Thatching|thatched]] and are [[listed building]]s, whose walls are painted with [[Whitewash|limewash]] that has been tinted creamy yellow with [[ochre]].<ref>{{NHLE |num=1057988 |desc=No 1 Lower Cottage and Greenbanks |access-date=26 January 2008}}</ref><ref>{{NHLE |num=1058025 |desc=Cottage (National Trust Estate No 68) |access-date=26 January 2008}}</ref><ref>{{NHLE |num=1345423 |desc=Selworthy Cottage and wall abutting on south front returned to road |access-date=26 January 2008}}</ref> On the hill above the village is the whitewashed 15th-century Church of All Saints, with a 14th-century tower. One of Allerford's main attractions is the much-photographed [[packhorse bridge]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Allerford Exmoor and the Exmoor National Park|url=http://www.everythingexmoor.org.uk/encyclopedia_detail.php?ENCid=63 |publisher=Everything Exmoor|access-date=23 May 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Allerford, Somerset|url=http://www.britainexpress.com/counties/somerset/az/Allerford.htm |publisher=Britain Express|access-date=23 May 2015}}</ref> Built as a crossing over the [[River Aller]] (from which the village gets its name), it is thought to be medieval in origin.<ref>{{NHLE |num=1058014 |desc=Packhorse Bridge |access-date=5 January 2008}}</ref> The village is also home to [[Allerford House]], childhood home of Admiral [[John Moresby]], who explored the coastline of [[New Guinea]] and for whom [[Port Moresby]], the capital city of [[Papua New Guinea]], was named. Other features of the village include thatched cottages, a forge and an old-fashioned [[red telephone box]]. There is also a Reading Room, built by the Acland family to foster adult education. One of the thatched cottages operated as the local Primary School between 1821 and 1981 and is now a museum containing the [[West Somerset Rural Life Museum and Victorian School]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.hornermill.co.uk/allerford/schoola.html |title=Allerford Museum|work=Horner Mill web site|access-date=5 May 2009}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cornucopia.org.uk/html/search/verb/ListIdentifiers/set/location/1727 |title=West Somerset Rural Life Museum|work=Cornucopia|publisher=Museums and Libraries Association|access-date=5 May 2009|url-status=dead|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20150923210552/http://www.cornucopia.org.uk/html/search/verb/ListIdentifiers/set/location/1727 |archive-date=23 September 2015|df=dmy-all}}</ref> The museum houses the West Somerset Photographic Archive.

The village of Luccombe lies at the foot of Dunkery Hill. Along with Stoke Pero and Horner it forms a civil parish. Horner is on the eastern bank of Horner Water on which there is a restored, but non-working, [[watermill]]. The river is crossed by two medieval [[packhorse]] bridges, one of which is known as Hacketty Way Bridge which is crossed by the [[Coleridge Way]].<ref>{{NHLE |num=1174852 |desc=Packhorse Bridge at NGR SS 8987 4608 |access-date=24 January 2009}}</ref><ref>{{NHLE |num=1057326 |desc=Hacketty Way Bridge |access-date=24 January 2009}}</ref> The parish [[Church of St Mary, Luccombe|Church of St Mary]] has a [[chancel]] dating from about 1300, with the nave and tower being added around 1450.<ref>{{NHLE |num=1057328 |desc=Church of St Mary |access-date=24 January 2009}}</ref> Stoke Pero Church has a 13th-century tower.<ref>{{NHLE |num=1174803 |desc=Stoke Pero Church |access-date=24 January 2009}}</ref> The [[Dovecot at Blackford Farm]] is part of the estate. It was built in the 11th century and is a [[Grade II* listed]] building,<ref>{{National Heritage List for England |num=1345406 |desc=Dovecot at Blackford Farm|access-date=6 April 2015}}</ref> and ancient monument.<ref>{{cite web|title=Dovecote at Little Blackford|url=http://www.somersetheritage.org.uk/record/34626 |work=Somerset Historic Environment Record|publisher=Somerset County Council|access-date=11 April 2014}}</ref><ref>{{National Heritage List for England |num=1020774 |desc=Dovecote at Little Blackford|access-date=6 April 2015}}</ref> It was attached to a mansion house which burnt down in 1875.<ref>{{cite web|title=Dovecote, Blackford Farm|url=http://www.exmoorher.co.uk/hbsmr-web/record.aspx?UID=MSO8017-Dovecote-Blackford-Farm&pageid=16&mid=9 |work=Exmoor Historic Environment Record|publisher=Exmoor National Park|access-date=10 April 2014}}</ref>

Since 2009 the estate has been one of three Multi-Objective Flood Management Demonstration Schemes, funded by the [[Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs]], to examine how changes in the management of river catchment areas can influence the incidence and severity of flooding in the area.<ref>{{cite web|title=Holnicote|url=http://ccmhub.net/case-studies/holnicote-case-studies/holnicote/ |publisher=Catchment Change Management Hub|access-date=19 October 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=The National Trust Holnicote Project |url=http://archive.defra.gov.uk/environment/flooding/documents/manage/multi-objective-fm-scheme-factsheet1.pdf |publisher=DEFRA |access-date=19 October 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20141019131916/http://archive.defra.gov.uk/environment/flooding/documents/manage/multi-objective-fm-scheme-factsheet1.pdf |archive-date=19 October 2014 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Holnicote Project|url=http://ecosystemsknowledge.net/resources/examples/holnicote |publisher=Ecosystems Knowledge Network|access-date=19 October 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Carrington|first1=Damian|title=Flood defenders go back to nature to keep vulnerable homes dry|url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2014/jan/10/flood-defence-nature-experiments |access-date=21 January 2015|work=Guardian|date=10 January 2014}}</ref> [[Beaver]]s were re-introduced to assist flood reduction.<ref>{{cite web |title=Beaver's new home at Holnicote |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/webarchive/https%3A%2F%2Fwww.bbc.co.uk%2Fblogs%2Fnatureuk%2Fentries%2Feafcf0bb-49df-4c7f-88ae-6b436b4bec3d |website=www.bbc.co.uk |publisher=[[Springwatch]] |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20210124155940/https://www.bbc.co.uk/blogs/natureuk/entries/eafcf0bb-49df-4c7f-88ae-6b436b4bec3d |archive-date=24 January 2021 |date=9 June 2020 |url-status=live}}</ref>

==House and outbuildings==
[[File:HolnicoteHouse CottageOrnee Selworthy Somerset.jpg|thumb|left|Holnicote House, the [[cottage orné]] hunting lodge built in about 1800 and burned down in 1851, predecessor of the present building]]

[[File:Medieval Gatehouse, Holnicote (geograph 4413937).jpg|thumb|160px|Gatehouse]]There have been at least four successive mansion houses at Holnicote. Limited information is available about the early buildings. One is known to have been built between 1493 and 1521, based on [[dendrochronology]] from surviving timbers. The Grade II* listed gatehouse and attached cottage were built together with a new house in the early 17th century.<ref>{{NHLE|num= 1173887| desc=  GATEHOUSE AND GATEHOUSE COTTAGE ADJOINING |access-date = 1 July 2015}}</ref> Following the purchase of the estate by the Blackford family in 1705, a new mansion house was built on the site of the previous structure.<ref name=exher22093>{{cite web|title=MEM22093 – Holnicote House|url=http://www.exmoorher.co.uk/hbsmr-web/record.aspx?UID=MEM22093-Holnicote-House|website=Exmoor Historic Environment Record|publisher=Exmoor National Park|access-date=15 December 2013}}</ref> Only the stable block from that building survives.<ref>{{National Heritage List for England |num=1295993 |desc=Stable block to Holnicote House|access-date=6 April 2015}}</ref> The house was destroyed by fire in 1779. The [[Acland baronets|Acland family]] re-built it as a thatched hunting lodge, which was also destroyed by fire in 1851,<ref>{{cite news|title=Holnicote fire|url=http://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0000361/18510906/023/0004|access-date=19 October 2014|work=Salisbury and Winchester Journal|date=6 September 1851| via = [[British Newspaper Archive]]|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and replaced in 1861. A kitchen extension was added in 1874.<ref name=exher22093/> The lodge was built in the 19th century.<ref>{{National Heritage List for England |num=1173840 |desc=Higher Lodge|access-date=6 April 2015}}</ref> The estate includes several cottages including Rose Bower<ref>{{National Heritage List for England |num=1173863 |desc=Rose Bower and No 53|access-date=6 April 2015}}</ref> and the 17th-century Butlers Cottage.<ref>{{National Heritage List for England |num=1345412 |desc=Butlers Cottage|access-date=6 April 2015}}</ref> An 18th-century [[Flemish bond]] red brick granary also exists on the estate.<ref>{{National Heritage List for England |num=1058024 |desc=Granary|access-date=6 April 2015}}</ref>

== Holnicote House in the 20th century ==
Holnicote House was donated to the [[National Trust]] by [[Richard Acland|Sir Richard Thomas Dyke Acland, 15th Baronet]]{{sfn|Dunning|1980|p=125}} of [[Killerton]] in Devon, whose ancestors had owned it since 1745.<ref name="BBC Holnicote">{{cite web |title=National Trust, Holnicote Estate |url=https://artuk.org/visit/venues/national-trust-holnicote-estate-4970 |access-date=21 January 2015 |website=[[Art UK]]}}</ref> In 1936 the lodge became a hotel, but was badly damaged by yet another fire in 1941.<ref>{{cite news |date=10 January 1941 |title=Holnicote House: Hotel Gutted Near Minehead |work=Western Times |url=http://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0000265/19410110/008/0002 |url-access=subscription |access-date=19 October 2014 |via=[[British Newspaper Archive]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |date=13 March 1936 |title=Hotel licence granted to Mr Richard Acland, M.P. |work=Exeter and Plymouth Gazette |url=http://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/viewer/bl/0000512/19360313/056/0009 |url-access=subscription |access-date=19 October 2014 |via=[[British Newspaper Archive]]}}</ref>

=== Mixed race children at Holnicote House during WW2 ===
[[File:Children_who_lived_at_Holnicote_House_during_the_1940s.jpg|thumb|right|Children of African American soldiers and white British women born during World War 2 who lived at Holnicote House until they were 5 years old.|alt=8 mixed race children standing in a row in a garden in the 1940s at Holnicote House in England. The children are wearing dresses or shorts.]]
In 1943, Holnicote House was requisitioned by [[Somerset County Council]], initially for use as a nursery for children evacuated from cities during World War 2. However, the council increasingly took children born to white British mothers and [[Military history of African Americans|Black American GI]] fathers, possibly as an intentional policy. American GIs, including Black American troops, were stationed all over Britain, with a heavy concentration in south-west England.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Smith |first=Graham |title=When Jim Crow met John Bull: Black American soldiers in World War II Britain |date=1987 |publisher=Tauris |isbn=0-312-01596-8 |oclc=17353377}}</ref><ref name=":02">{{Cite book |last=Bland |first=Lucy |title=Britain's 'brown babies' : the stories of children born to black GIs and white women in the Second World War |date=2020 |isbn=978-1-5261-5405-7 |location=Manchester |oclc=1159422997}}</ref> The children often arrived at Holnicote House as babies, some being only a few days or weeks old. This early placement is likely because at least two-thirds of the babies had married mothers. By 1948, there were 45 mixed race children of Black GIs in [[Somerset]], of whom nearly half were placed in Holnicote House.<ref name=":02" /><ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last1=Caballero |first1=Chamion |title=Mixed Race Britain in the Twentieth Century |last2=Aspinall |first2=Peter J. |publisher=Palgrave Macmillan |year=2018 |isbn=978-1-137-33927-0 |location=London |language=English}}</ref>

Somerset appears to be the only county council which provided homes explicitly for babies born to Black GIs. As Holnicote House was used as a nursery, children were only cared for there up to the age of five, after which they were fostered, adopted or sent to homes for older children. The children who were fostered at Holnicote House tended to be cared for by young nursery nurses. [[Lucy Bland|Professor Lucy Bland]], who interviewed over sixty children born to white mothers and Black American GI fathers for her 2019 book ''Britain's 'Brown Babies'', talked to five people who were raised at Holnicote House, as well as three nursery nurses who worked there. All spoke very fondly about their time there.<ref name=":02" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Brown Babies Archive |url=https://mixedmuseum.org.uk/brown-babies/ |access-date=2022-12-14 |website=The Mixed Museum |language=en}}</ref>

On 23 August 1948, [[Life (magazine)|''Life'' magazine]] published a feature entitled ‘The Babies They Left Behind Them’. This article, which was accompanied by a photo of children from Holnicote House, attracted international public interest in the issue of Britain’s ‘[[Brown Babies|brown babies]]’ as the estimated 2,000 children from the relationships between Black GIs and white British women were dubbed by the Black American press.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Babies They Left Behind Them |url=https://exhibition.mixedmuseum.org.uk/museum/timeline/the-babies-they-left-behind-them |access-date=2022-12-14 |website=www.mixedmuseum.org.uk}}</ref><ref name=":02" /><ref name=":1" />

The house is now operated as a hotel.<ref>{{cite web|title=Holnicote House|url=http://www.holnicotehouse.co.uk/|publisher=HF holidays|access-date=19 October 2014|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://archive.today/20141019115219/http://www.holnicotehouse.co.uk/|archive-date=19 October 2014|df=dmy-all}}</ref>

6030554.title: King John's Hunting Lodge, Axbridge
6030554.extract:
King John's Hunting Lodge is a wool-merchant's house built c. 1468, long after the death of King John in 1216, in Axbridge, a town in the English county of Somerset. It is a jettied timber-frame building of three storeys, occupying a corner plot on the town square. The building has served a variety of purposes with shops on the ground floor and workshops and living quarters on the first and second floors. At one time part of the building was occupied by the King's Head Inn; a sculpture of a king's head, which acted as a sign for the pub, is preserved within and a replica is attached to the outside. The lodge was bequeathed to the National Trust in 1971, and repairs were undertaken to reverse significant deterioration to the building.
The house is leased by the National Trust to Axbridge and District Museum Trust, who operate it as a local museum which includes exhibits relating to local geology and history from the Neolithic to World War II. It is a Grade II* listed building.

'''King John's Hunting Lodge''' is a [[wool]]-merchant's house built {{circa|1468}},{{cn|date=January 2026}} long after the death of [[King John of England|King John]] in 1216, in [[Axbridge]], a town in the English county of [[Somerset]]. It is a [[Jettying|jettied]] [[timber framing|timber-frame]] building of three storeys, occupying a corner plot on the town square. The building has served a variety of purposes with shops on the ground floor and workshops and living quarters on the first and second floors. At one time part of the building was occupied by the King's Head Inn; a sculpture of a king's head, which acted as a sign for the pub, is preserved within and a replica is attached to the outside. The lodge was bequeathed to the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] in 1971, and repairs were undertaken to reverse significant deterioration to the building.

The house is leased by the National Trust to Axbridge and District Museum Trust, who operate it as a local museum which includes exhibits relating to local geology and history from the [[Neolithic]] to [[World War II]]. It is a Grade II* [[Listed building (United Kingdom)|listed building]].<ref name=nhle>{{NHLE | desc=King John's Hunting Lodge (Axbridge Museum) | num=1059142 | access-date=23 December 2013}}</ref>

== History ==
[[File:King John's Hunting Lodge, Axbridge stairs.jpg|thumb|left|upright|Internal stairs]]
In 1340 the site of the present building was occupied by a building belonging to John Oldeway. It contained shops and was called "the stockhouse".<ref name=tc/> The current building, which was constructed around 1460, was occupied by shops on the ground floor, living areas and workshops on the first floor, and storage and sleeping areas on the second floor.<ref name=reid/>

The house is the finest of a number of [[timber-frame]] houses in the High Street and The Square.<ref name=reid/> The three-storey building is [[Jettying|jettied]] on two adjacent sides and has three [[gable]]s on the longer side.  On the first and second floors curved brackets can be seen which support the floor above.<ref name=nhle/> The structure is based around a single wooden post, known as a [[king post]], at the front corner of the building, which supports the floor boards and the horizontal [[dragon beam]]s that carry the projection of the upper floors at each level.<ref>{{cite web |title=Ground floor |url=http://www.beewhizz.co.uk/KJHL/WP/?page_id=25 |publisher=The Axbridge and District Museum Trust |access-date=24 December 2013}}</ref>

In the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, the building housed a succession of shops and underwent various changes which contributed to its physical decline.  A Miss Ripley bought the building in 1930, and used it to store her collection of antiques until 1968, allowing the public to see her collection once a year.  She bequeathed it to the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] in 1971, who undertook the works necessary to make it fit for visitors and saved it from probable destruction.<ref name=tc/><ref name=lis>{{cite news |url=http://www.somersetguardian.co.uk/Light-shed-mystery-lodge/story-17882120-detail/story.html |title=Light is shed on mystery of lodge |work=Somerset Guardian |date=17 January 2013 |access-date=30 April 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140502034529/http://www.somersetguardian.co.uk/Light-shed-mystery-lodge/story-17882120-detail/story.html |archive-date=2 May 2014 |df=dmy-all }}</ref>

In overhauling the structure of the premises, the National Trust restored its medieval character by recreating on the ground floor the appearance of arcaded stalls opening onto the street, and the sixteenth-century decoration of the upstairs windows, although this caused a dilemma as it required the removal of fine 18th-century windows.<ref>{{cite web |title=King John's Hunting Lodge |publisher=Axbridge and District Museum |url=http://www.kingjohnshuntinglodge.co.uk/ |access-date=25 August 2006}}</ref><ref name=reid>{{cite book |last=Reid |first=Robert Douglas |title=Some buildings of Mendip |year=1979 |publisher=The Mendip Society |isbn=0-905459-16-4 |pages=10–13 }}</ref>

The origin of the name is unclear as it was not built until long after the reign of [[John, King of England|King John]], who died in 1216. Its present name first appeared in a 1915 publication, ''The Heart of Mendip'' by Francis Knight, when it was being run as a saddler's shop. The royal part of the name may have come from the fact that there was a carved king's head on the building, from a time when ''The King's Head Inn'' occupied part of the premises, but whether this represented King John or another king is not known.<ref name=tc>{{cite web |title=The Museum |url=http://www.axbridge-tc.gov.uk/trust/TrustMuseumArtefacts.html |publisher=Axbridge Town Council |access-date=23 December 2013 |archive-date=24 December 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131224205229/http://www.axbridge-tc.gov.uk/trust/TrustMuseumArtefacts.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> The head was attached to one corner of the exterior, but is now inside the building, and a replica placed on the outside.<ref name=nhle/><ref>{{cite web |title=The Medieval Burgh of Axbridge |publisher=Time Travel-Britain.com |url=http://www.timetravel-britain.com/06/May/axbridge.shtml |access-date=25 August 2006}}</ref>

The property is owned by the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] and run as a local history museum by Axbridge and District Museum Trust with support from Somerset County Museums Service and Axbridge Archaeological and Local History Society. Until 2011 funding was received from [[Sedgemoor|Sedgemoor District Council]], but this was withdrawn and an entry charge introduced to help pay for the running costs.<ref>{{cite news |last=Egginton |first=Steve |title=Town rallies round its museum |work=Mendip Times |date=May 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=King John's Hunting Lodge – National Trust |url=http://www.culture24.org.uk/sw000187 |publisher=Culture 24 |access-date=23 December 2013}}</ref>

The museum aims to illustrate the history, geology and community of Axbridge and the surrounding area (the area of the old [[Axbridge Rural District]], which included many neighbouring villages such as [[Cheddar, Somerset|Cheddar]], [[Wedmore]], [[Mark, Somerset|Mark]] and [[Winscombe]]). There is a core of long-term and permanent exhibits, reviewed regularly for possible changes, updates, and revised displays and information, and there is a programme of temporary exhibitions to reflect many aspects of local life and heritage.<ref name=exhib/>

Each room has a specific theme, which includes aspects of local history such as life during [[World War II]], and aspects of law and order. Another exhibition shows local geology and archaeological finds from local caves.<ref name=exhib>{{cite web |title=Exhibitions |url=http://www.beewhizz.co.uk/KJHL/WP/?page_id=40 |publisher=The Axbridge and District Museum Trust |access-date=24 December 2013}}</ref> The exhibits include a fine flint flake which has been identified from the [[Neolithic]] occupation of [[Ebbor Gorge]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Bond |first=Clive Jonathon |title=The later upper Palaeolithic open sites and settlement trajectories. The evidence from the Mendip Hills, south-west Britain |url=http://www.naturalsciences.be/mars/groups/fnrs-contact-group/notae-praehistoricae/NP_pdf/NP33/np33_179-192_mendiphills_bond_201113_600-p.pdf |journal=Notae Praehistoricae |year=2013 |volume=33 |pages=179–192 |archive-date=24 February 2014 |access-date=30 April 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140224004458/http://www.naturalsciences.be/mars/groups/fnrs-contact-group/notae-praehistoricae/NP_pdf/NP33/np33_179-192_mendiphills_bond_201113_600-p.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> The museum also displays paintings of local scenes and objects including a clock made by John Bilbie of the [[Bilbie family]], who lived in Axbridge, and a merchants' table known as a "nail", similar to those outside [[The Exchange, Bristol#Nails|The Exchange in Bristol]] which were made with a flat top and raised edges to prevent coins from tumbling onto the pavement.<ref>{{cite web |title=Gallery |url=http://www.beewhizz.co.uk/KJHL/WP/?page_id=132 |publisher=The Axbridge and District Museum Trust |access-date=24 December 2013}}</ref>

13962744.title: Lytes Cary
13962744.extract:
Lytes Cary is a manor house with associated chapel and gardens near Charlton Mackrell and Somerton in Somerset, England. The property, owned by the National Trust, has parts dating to the 14th century, with other sections dating to the 15th, 16th, 18th, and 20th centuries. "Yet all parts blend to perfection with one another and with the gentle sunny landscape that surrounds them," comments Nikolaus Pevsner. The House is listed as Grade I by English Heritage.
The chapel predates the existing house, having been built around 1343, and functioned as a chantry chapel, where masses could be said for the souls of the family, both living and dead. The great hall was added in the 15th century and the Oriel Room in the 16th. Various renovations were undertaken during the 16th and 17th centuries after which the house fell into disrepair with the north range being demolished by the early 19th century. In 1907 Sir Walter Jenner of the Jenner baronets bought the house and restored it in a period style, furnishing it with fine 17th century and 18th century oak furniture, antique tapestries and fabrics modelled after medieval textiles, along with historic and period paintings. On his death in 1948 he left the house to the National Trust.
The gardens are listed as Grade II on the Register of Historic Parks and Gardens of special historic interest in England. The original 17th-century gardens have disappeared. However, the Jenners laid them out in an Arts and Crafts style with a series of 'rooms', which are separated from each other by high, neatly clipped box and yew hedges. These are complemented by ponds and walks in and between each of the 'rooms'.

The '''Priest's House''' is a [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]]-owned property in [[Muchelney]], in the English county of [[Somerset]]. It has been designated as a grade I [[listed building]].<ref name=hhle>{{NHLE|desc=The Priest's house |num=1056574 |access-date=14 December 2013}}</ref> The house was built in the early 14th century by the nearby [[Muchelney Abbey]] to house the parish priest.

Over the centuries the house deteriorated and was adapted for use as a school. In the late 19th century it rented as storage by a farmer. In the early 20th century the [[Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings]] campaigned for its restoration and it was then taken over by the National Trust. The thatched stone building is rented to a tenant and has limited public access.

==History==

The Priest's House was built by the nearby [[Muchelney Abbey]] around 1308 for the parish priest.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Bettey|first1=J. H.|title=Wessex from Ad1000|date=2014|publisher=Routledge|isbn=9781317871859|page=93|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jWHXAwAAQBAJ&q=Priest%27s+House%2C+Muchelney&pg=PA93}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=25 August 2007 |title=Living in history: Priest's House, Muchelney |url=http://www.somerset-life.co.uk/out-about/places/living_in_history_priest_s_house_muchelney_1_1630366#article-comments |access-date=14 December 2013 |newspaper=Somerset Life}}</ref><ref name=pantin>{{cite journal |year=1957 |title=Medieval Priests' Houses in South-West England |journal=Medieval Archaeology |volume=1 |last=Pantin|first=William Abel|authorlink=William Abel Pantin |publisher=Society for Medieval Archaeology |pages=118–146 |doi=10.1080/00766097.1957.11735386 |url= https://archaeologydataservice.ac.uk/archiveDS/archiveDownload?t=arch-769-1/dissemination/pdf/vol01/1_118_146.pdf}}</ref> The vicarage was valued at £10 per annum in 1535.<ref name=pantin/> The building was said to be "ruinous" in 1608.<ref name=hhle/> It was used by the vicar or curate until around 1840, when the house was used as a cellar and later as a school.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.british-history.ac.uk/report.aspx?compid=66485 |title=Parishes: Muchelney |author=R. W. Dunning (editor), A. P. Baggs, R. J. E. Bush, Margaret Tomlinson |publisher=Institute of Historical Research |date=1974 |work=A History of the County of Somerset: Volume 3 |access-date=20 April 2014 }}</ref>

In the late 19th century it was rented by a farmer for storage. Because of its poor condition it was recommended for demolition in both 1896 and 1901. The [[Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings]] organised a public appeal to raise money for repairs to which [[Jane Morris]], [[Thomas Hardy]] and [[George Bernard Shaw]] contributed. As the funding for the restoration was no longer an issue the building was acquired, in 1911,<ref name=hhle/> by the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] who employed Ernest Barnsley of the [[Barnsley brothers]], the [[Arts and Crafts movement]] master builders, to design and the work. It was carried out by [[Norman Jewson]] and [[William Weir (architect)|William Weir]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Norman Jewson, architect|url=http://www.owlpen.com/content/norman-jewson|publisher=Owlpen Manor Estate|access-date=20 April 2014|archive-date=21 April 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140421082519/http://www.owlpen.com/content/norman-jewson|url-status=dead}}</ref> The work left in place and strengthened earlier structures where possible but added new aspects including a stone [[buttress]] and a kitchen range.<ref name="Stratton 1997 24–26">{{cite book|last=Stratton|first=Michael|title=Structure and Style: Conserving Twentieth Century Buildings|date=1997|publisher=Taylor & Francis|isbn=9780419217404|pages=24–26|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xquZeaoRcnQC&q=Priest%27s+House%2C+Muchelney&pg=PA26}}</ref>

In the 1990s and 2000s the building underwent further structural repairs, including the replacement of the timber structure supporting the roof and was rethatched with grant aid from [[English Heritage]].<ref name="Stratton 1997 24–26"/><ref>{{cite web |title=Muchelney Somerset Grass roots conservation |url=https://www.english-heritage.org.uk/publications/conservation-bulletin-42/66muchelneysomerset-localconservation.pdf |work=Conservation Bulletin 42 |publisher=English Heritage |access-date=14 December 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=The Priest's House|url=http://www.architecton.co.uk/PAGES/488-Brochure-web.pdf|publisher=Architecton|access-date=20 April 2014|archive-date=21 April 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140421064152/http://www.architecton.co.uk/PAGES/488-Brochure-web.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> Today the National Trust rent it to a tenant who provides limited access to the public.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ross |first=David |title=Muchelney Priest's House |url=https://www.britainexpress.com/attractions.htm?attraction=3253 |publisher=Britain Express |access-date=14 December 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Priest's House, Muchelney |url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/priests-house-muchelney/ |publisher=National Trust |access-date=14 December 2013}}</ref>

==Architecture==

The two-storey thatched [[hall house]] is made of local stone with [[hamstone]] dressings. Externally the house measures {{convert|51|ft}} by {{convert|22|ft}} wide.<ref name=pantin/> It has four bays along the south front which incorporates original Gothic doorway and tracery windows.<ref>{{cite book|last=Greeves|first=Lydia|title=Houses of the National Trust|date=2008|publisher=National Trust|isbn=9781907892486|pages=388–389}}</ref>  Inside is a 15th-century fireplace.<ref name=hhle/>

The original hall went from floor to roof, however in the 16th century a ceiling was added dividing it into two floors. This also involved changes to the original windows.<ref name=pantin/> The hall has a [[cruck]] roof with a saddle apex typical of the 14th century.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Penoyre|first1=Jane|title=Traditional Houses of Somerset|date=2005|publisher=Somerset Books|isbn=978-0861834075|page=100}}</ref>

14141803.title: King Alfred's Tower
14141803.extract:
Alfred's Tower is a folly in Somerset, England, on the edge of the border with Wiltshire, on the Stourhead estate. The tower stands on Kingsettle Hill and belongs to the National Trust. It is designated as a Grade I listed building.
Henry Hoare II planned the tower in the 1760s to commemorate the end of the Seven Years' War against France and the accession of King George III, and it was erected near the site of Egbert's Stone, where it is believed that Alfred the Great, King of Wessex, rallied the Anglo-Saxons in 878 before the Battle of Edington. The tower was damaged by an aeroplane in 1944 and restored in the 1980s.
The 49-metre-high (161 ft) triangular tower has a hollow centre and is climbed by means of a spiral staircase in one of the corner projections. It has a statue of King Alfred and a dedication inscription.

|archive-date=23 October 2021 |website=alfredstower.info |via=Internet Archive}} It was designated as a Grade I [[listed building]] in 1961. Restoration work in 1986 included the use of a [[Westland Wessex|Wessex helicopter]] to lower a {{cvt|300|kg}} piece of masonry onto the top. The statue of King Alfred was also restored at this time, including the replacement of his missing right forearm. ==Architecture== The triangular tower is over {{cvt|40|m}} high with a girth of {{cvt|51|m}}. Each of the three corners of the triangular structure has a round projection. The centre of the tower is hollow, and to stop birds from entering the space a mesh has been added at roof level. The viewing platform, which has a [[crenellation|crenellated]] [[parapet]] and offers a view over the surrounding countryside, is reached by a 205-step spiral staircase at the corner furthest from the entrance. The brick tower has [[Chicksgrove Quarry|Chilmark stone]] dressings and is surmounted by an embattled parapet.{{cite web|title=Alfred's Tower, Kingsettle Hill (South side), Brewham|url=http://www.somersetheritage.org.uk/record/50734|work=Somerset Historic Environment Record|publisher=Somerset County Council|access-date=15 May 2014}}{{cite web|title=Alfred's Tower, Brewham|url=http://www.somersetheritage.org.uk/record/55478|work=Somerset Historic Environment Record|publisher=Somerset County Council|access-date=15 May 2014}} The south-east face of the tower has a [[Ogive#Architecture|Gothic-arched]] entrance door, a statue of King Alfred, and a stone panel bearing an inscription (see below). This is the face that most visitors see first when walking from [[Stourhead]] garden or from the nearby car park. File:The top of Alfred's Tower - geograph.org.uk - 1310883.jpg|The turret above the stair-tower at the top of the tower File:Plaque carrying inscription on King Alfred's Tower.png|Plaque {{cvt|8|m}} above the entrance File:KingAlfredsTowerStatue.png|Statue of King Alfred above the entrance ===Inscription=== Around the Stourhead estate are several inscriptions. The plaque of the inscription is in poor condition and needs restoration. It was drafted in 1762 and installed in 1772.{{cite journal|last=Turner|first=James|journal=The Art Bulletin|date= March 1979|volume=61|issue=1|pages=68–77 | title=The Structure of Henry Hoare's Stourhead|jstor=3049865|doi=10.2307/3049865}} The stone tablet above the door on the east face of the tower reads:
ALFRED THE GREAT AD 879 on this Summit Erected his Standard Against Danish Invaders To him We owe The Origin of Juries The Establishment of a Militia The Creation of a Naval Force ALFRED The Light of a Benighted Age Was a Philosopher and a Christian The Father of his People The Founder of the English MONARCHY and LIBERTY
==In popular culture== The tower is mentioned in [[Thomas Hardy]]'s poem "Channel Firing" (written in April 1914) as a place "far inland".Hardy, Thomas. 41509642.title: Sand Point and Middle Hope
41509642.extract:
Sand Point in Somerset, England, is the peninsula stretching out from Middle Hope, an 84.1-hectare (208-acre) biological and geological Site of Special Scientific Interest. It lies to the north of the village of Kewstoke, and the stretch of coastline called Sand Bay north of the town of Weston-super-Mare.  On a clear day it commands views over Flat Holm, of the Bristol Channel, South Wales, Clevedon, the Second Severn Crossing and the Severn Bridge.
Some sources treat Sand Point as the lower limit of the Severn Estuary and its boundary with the Bristol Channel, although definitions of these areas vary and are often ambiguous. The Living Levels Partnership use a definition that draws a line between Sand Point and Lavernock Point in South Wales.
Middle Hope is a sequence of carboniferous limestone with unusual geological features including a Pleistocene-aged fossil cliff and as a result has been designated as a regionally important geological site. The underlying geology and soil types support scarce plants such as the  smallflower buttercup, honewort, Cheddar pink and Somerset hair grass. Human use of the sites is shown by a bowl barrow and disc barrow from late Neolithic or Bronze Age and the site of a likely motte-and-bailey castle. Woodspring Priory, a former Augustinian priory which was founded in the early 13th century, sits just inland of the rocky promontory. The priory and surrounding land is owned by the National Trust and is a popular place for walking.

'''Sand Point''' in [[Somerset]], England, is the peninsula stretching out from '''Middle Hope''', an {{convert|84.1|ha|adj=on}} [[biological and geological Site of Special Scientific Interest]]. It lies to the north of the village of [[Kewstoke]], and the stretch of coastline called [[Sand Bay]] north of the town of [[Weston-super-Mare]].  On a clear day it commands views over [[Flat Holm]], of the [[Bristol Channel]], [[South Wales]], [[Clevedon]], the [[Second Severn Crossing]] and the [[Severn Bridge]].

Some sources treat Sand Point as the lower limit of the [[Severn Estuary]] and its boundary with the Bristol Channel, although definitions of these areas vary and are often ambiguous.<ref>{{cite web |title=Across the waters Implementation of the UK Marine and Coastal Access Act and devolved marine legislation: cross-border case studies | date=December 2009 |url=https://wcl.org.uk/docs/2009/Joint_Links_AcrosstheWaters_SevernEstuary_BristolChannel_Dec09.pdf | quote="There is no defined boundary between the Severn Estuary and the Bristol Channel. The Welsh 'Mor Hafren' or 'The Severn Sea' includes the relatively enclosed waters to the line of the proposed barrage extending from Brean Down via Steep Holm and Flat Holm to Lavernock Point."}}</ref> The Living Levels Partnership use a definition that draws a line between Sand Point and [[Lavernock#Lavernock Point|Lavernock Point]] in South [[Wales]].<ref>{{cite web |title=The Severn Estuary |url=https://www.livinglevels.org.uk/severn-estuary |website=Living Levels}}</ref>

Middle Hope is a sequence of [[carboniferous]] [[limestone]] with unusual geological features including a [[Pleistocene]]-aged fossil cliff and as a result has been designated as a [[regionally important geological site]]. The underlying geology and soil types support scarce plants such as the  [[Ranunculus parviflorus|smallflower buttercup]], [[Trinia glauca|honewort]], [[Dianthus gratianopolitanus|Cheddar pink]] and [[Koeleria vallesiana|Somerset hair grass]]. Human use of the sites is shown by a [[bowl barrow]] and [[disc barrow]] from late [[Neolithic]] or [[Bronze Age]] and the site of a likely [[motte-and-bailey castle]]. [[Woodspring Priory]], a former [[Augustinians|Augustinian]] [[priory]] which was founded in the early 13th century, sits just inland of the rocky promontory. The priory and surrounding land is owned by the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] and is a popular place for walking.

==Geology==
[[File:Sand Point and Middle Hope 14.JPG|thumb|left|The cliffs and rocky beach at Middle Hope]]
At Middle Hope a sequence of [[carboniferous]] [[limestone]] is exposed, which includes thick [[Volcano|volcanic]] [[tuff]]s and [[lava]]s, demonstrating [[Tournaisian]] carbonate sections.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Prudden|first1=Hugh|title=Somerset Geology — A Good Rock Guide|url=http://people.bath.ac.uk/exxbgs/Somerset_Good_Rock_Guide.pdf|website=University of Bath|publisher=Bath Geological Society|access-date=8 March 2015}}</ref> The site contains a [[Pleistocene]]-aged fossil cliff and shore platform.<ref name="sssicitation">{{cite web|url=http://www.english-nature.org.uk/citation/citation_photo/1002814.pdf|title=Middle Hope|work=SSSI citation sheet|publisher=English Nature|access-date=31 October 2008}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Faulkner|first1=T.J.|title=The early Carboniferous (Courceyan) Middle Hope volcanics of Weston-super-Mare: development and demise of an offshore volcanic high|journal=Proceedings of the Geologists' Association|date=1989|volume=100|issue=1|pages=93–106|doi=10.1016/S0016-7878(89)80068-9}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=North Somerset Landscape Character Assessment|url=https://www.n-somerset.gov.uk/Environment/Planning_policy_and-research/Documents/Supplementary%20planning%20documents/North%20Somerset%20landscape%20character%20assessment%20supplementary%20planning%20document%20(pdf).pdf|publisher=North Somerset Council|access-date=8 March 2015|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140715102335/https://www.n-somerset.gov.uk/Environment/Planning_policy_and-research/Documents/Supplementary%20planning%20documents/North%20Somerset%20landscape%20character%20assessment%20supplementary%20planning%20document%20(pdf).pdf|archive-date=15 July 2014|df=dmy-all}}</ref> These features have led to the designation of Middle Hope as a [[regionally important geological site]] (RIGS).<ref name=RIGS/>

The raised beach of wave-cut platforms has been created by changes in sea level of the [[Bristol Channel]] since the [[Quaternary|Quaternary period]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Severn Estuary|url=http://www.severn-boating.co.uk/estuary.htm|publisher=Severn Boating|access-date=15 December 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=North Somerset Landscape Character Assessment|url=https://www.n-somerset.gov.uk/Environment/Planning_policy_and-research/Documents/Supplementary%20planning%20documents/North%20Somerset%20landscape%20character%20assessment%20supplementary%20planning%20document%20(pdf).pdf|publisher=North Somerset Council|access-date=14 July 2014|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140715102335/https://www.n-somerset.gov.uk/Environment/Planning_policy_and-research/Documents/Supplementary%20planning%20documents/North%20Somerset%20landscape%20character%20assessment%20supplementary%20planning%20document%20(pdf).pdf|archive-date=15 July 2014|df=dmy-all}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Somerset|url=http://www.naturalengland.org.uk/ourwork/conservation/geodiversity/englands/counties/area_ID30.aspx|publisher=Natural 2014|df=dmy-all}}</ref> The arrangement of volcanic and sedimentary rocks, including the [[Black Rock Limestone]], illustrates the events of 350 million years ago.<ref>{{cite web|title=Middle Hope, Kewstoke, Somerset|url=http://avonrigsoutcrop.blogspot.co.uk/2013/03/rigs-of-month-march-middle-hope.html|publisher=Avon RIGS Group|access-date=14 July 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=OGU fieldtrip to Middle Hope|url=http://www.bris.ac.uk/chemistry/research/ogu/news/2013/23.html|publisher=University of Bristol|access-date=8 March 2015}}</ref> The [[Stratum|strata]] have been tilted and compressed during the [[variscan orogeny]].<ref name=RIGS>{{cite web|title=RIGS of the Month — March Middle Hope, Kewstoke, Somerset|url=http://avonrigsoutcrop.blogspot.co.uk/2013/03/rigs-of-month-march-middle-hope.html|publisher=Avon RIGS group|access-date=8 March 2015}}</ref>

==Flora==
Among scarce plants found on Sand Point are [[Ranunculus parviflorus|smallflower buttercup]],<ref>{{cite book|last1=Green|first1=Ian P.|last2=Higgins|first2=Rupert J.|last3=Kitchen|first3=Mark A R.|last4=Kitchen|first4=C.|editor-last=Myles|editor-first=Sarah L.|title=The Flora of the Bristol Region|date=2000|publisher=Pisces Publications|isbn=978-1874357186|page=66}}</ref> and [[Trinia glauca|honewort]].<ref>{{cite book|last1=Green|first1=Ian P.|last2=Higgins|first2=Rupert J.|last3=Kitchen|first3=Mark A R.|last4=Kitchen|first4=C.|editor-last=Myles|editor-first=Sarah L.|title=The Flora of the Bristol Region|date=2000|publisher=Pisces Publications|isbn=978-1874357186|page=161}}</ref> The range of soils at the site support various flora and fauna. The calcareous grassland is dominated by [[Festuca]] species and [[Dactylis glomerata]], while the scrub towards the west of the site is dominated by [[Crataegus monogyna|hawthorn]] ''(Crataegus monogyna)'' and [[Prunus spinosa|blackthorn]] ''(Prunus spinosa)'', while that to the east consists of [[Ulex europaeus|common gorse]] ''(Ulex europaeus)'' and [[Blackberry|bramble]] ''(Rubus fruticosus agg)''.<ref name="sssicitation"/> Less common plants include the [[Dianthus gratianopolitanus|cheddar pink]] ''(Dianthus gratianopolitanus)'' and [[Koeleria vallesiana|Somerset hair grass]] ''(Koeleria vallesiana)''.<ref>{{cite web|title=2012 Newsletter Issue No.13|url=http://www.somersetrareplantsgroup.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2014/11/2012-Newsletter-13-PDF.pdf|publisher=Somerset Rare Plants Group|access-date=10 May 2018}}</ref>

==History==
[[File:Sand Point and Middle Hope 17.JPG|thumb|The [[triangulation station]] and site of the [[bowl barrow]] and [[disc barrow]]]]
Evidence of early human occupation is provided by a [[bowl barrow]] and [[disc barrow]] from the late [[Neolithic]] or [[Bronze Age]] that have been identified on the higher ground. The bowl barrow is {{convert|10|m}} in diameter and approximately {{convert|0.5|m}} high. Slightly west of the bowl barrow is a disc barrow surrounded by a bank and ditch which enclose an area about {{convert|8|m}} across. These are situated at the highest point where the [[Ordnance Survey]] have constructed a [[triangulation station]].<ref>{{NHLE|desc=Bowl barrow and disc barrow 600 m NNW of Sandpoint Farm|num=1008115|access-date=8 March 2015}}</ref>

A [[motte-and-bailey castle]] may have been constructed after the [[Norman conquest of England|Norman Conquest]].<ref>{{NHLE|desc=Motte and bailey castle 650 m NNW of Sandpoint Farm|num=1008114|access-date=16 September 2014}}</ref> The site is known as Castle Mound or Castle Batch and can be seen as a {{convert|2|m}} high mound which is approximately {{convert|30|m}} in diameter and marked by a ditch on the landward eastern edge.<ref>{{PastScape|mname=|mnumber=192646|access-date=8 March 2015}}</ref> The mound was damaged by the construction of a building during [[World War II]]. The medieval date for the construction is in doubt with some sources suggesting that the mound may have been a watchtower constructed in the 16th century.<ref>{{cite web|title=Castle Mound ( Castle Batch), Sand Point and Middle Hope|url=http://archaeologydataservice.ac.uk/archsearch/record.jsf?titleId=1786937|publisher=Archaeology Data Service|access-date=8 March 2015}}</ref><ref name=NTwalk>{{cite web|title=Sand Point & Middlehope, Somerset|url=http://www.walk4life.info/sites/default/files/walkdocs/walkdoc-5289.pdf|publisher=National Trust|access-date=14 July 2014}}</ref><ref name=ntinfo>{{cite web|title=Sand Point and Middle Hope|url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/article-1356396397972/|publisher=National Trust|access-date=14 July 2014|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131215230033/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/article-1356396397972/|archive-date=15 December 2013|df=dmy-all}}</ref> The walls of the sheep fold were built by prisoners from the [[Napoleonic Wars]].<ref name=NTwalk/> Hope Cove on the northern coast had a reputation for smuggling as it was "well away from the men of [[HM Customs and Excise]]".<ref>{{cite book|last1=Body|first1=Geoff|last2=Gallop|first2=Roy|title=Any Muddy Bottom: A History of Somerset's Waterborne Trade|date=2015|publisher=History Press|isbn=978-0750961639|page=85}}</ref>

[[Woodspring Priory]] was an [[Augustinians|Augustinian]] [[priory]].<ref>{{NHLE|desc=Woodspring Priory and associated fishponds and field system|num=1012722|access-date=15 July 2014}}</ref> It was founded by William de Courtney, in the early 13th century, and dedicated to [[Thomas Becket]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Local History|url=http://kewstokevillage.com/?page_id=52|publisher=Kewstoke Village|access-date=16 July 2014}}</ref> The small community built a church and monastic lodgings during the next hundred years. They were [[Canons Regular#Victorine Canons and the Gallican Congregation|Victorine Canons]] who were influenced by the [[Cistercians]] emphasis on manual labour and self-sufficiency. As a result, the clerks who had taken holy orders worked on the farm, as well as providing clergy for surrounding churches.<ref>{{cite book|last=Greenwood|first=Charles|title=Famous Houses of the West Country|year=1977|publisher=Kingsmead Press|location=Bath|isbn=978-0901571878|pages=109–111}}</ref> Despite endowments of land the priory was not wealthy until the 15th century when further building work, including the current priory church, infirmary and barn was undertaken. It was [[Dissolution of the Monasteries|dissolved]] in 1536 and then owned by local noblemen and leased to local farmers.<ref>{{cite book|last=Dickens|first=Arthur Geoffrey|author-link=Arthur Geoffrey Dickens|title=The English Reformation|edition=2nd|location=London|publisher=B. T. Batsford|year=1989|isbn=978-0271028682}}</ref> In 1969 the priory was taken over by the [[Landmark Trust]] who spent 20 years on restoration work, and since the 1990s have rented out the farmhouse as holiday accommodation.<ref>{{cite web|title=Woodspring Priory — Restoration|url=http://www.landmarktrust.org.uk/our-landmarks/properties/woodspring-priory-13260/#tabs=2|publisher=Landmark Trust|access-date=15 July 2014|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140718155544/http://www.landmarktrust.org.uk/our-landmarks/properties/woodspring-priory-13260/#tabs=2|archive-date=18 July 2014|df=dmy-all}}</ref> The surviving buildings include the priory church, which was a 15th-century replacement for the earlier 13th century structure, infirmary, barn and 16th century prior's lodging which was converted into a farmhouse. The whole site was arranged around a central [[cloister]] from which only the east wall and west wall of the [[chapter house]] remain, the [[sacristy]], refectory, chapter house, lady chapel and parlour having been demolished.<ref>{{NHLE|desc=East Cloister Wall|num=1302945|access-date=15 July 2014}}</ref><ref>{{NHLE|desc=West Wall of Chapter House Range|num=1320653|access-date=15 July 2014}}</ref><ref>{{NHLE|desc=Infirmary|num=1156326|access-date=15 July 2014}}</ref>

Because of the biological and geological interest the site was designated as a [[Site of Special Scientific Interest]] in 1952.<ref name="sssicitation"/> In 1968 the priory and adjoining land of Middle Hope was purchased by the National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty as part of [[Project Neptune (National Trust)|Project Neptune]].<ref>{{cite book|last1=Tomalin|first1=David John|last2=Crook|first2=Christopher|title=Woodspring Priory|date=2007|publisher=The Landmark Trust}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last1=Longman|first1=Tim|title=Archaeological Watching Brief at Woodspring Priory|url=http://archaeologydataservice.ac.uk/archiveDS/archiveDownload?t=arch-918-1/dissemination/pdf/bristola1-68934_1.pdf|website=Archaeology Data Services|publisher=Bristol and Region Archaeological Services|date=16 March 2010|access-date=15 July 2014}}</ref>

During World War II weapons were tested at Sand Point,<ref name=ntinfo/> in association with the base at [[Birnbeck Pier]] which was commissioned as "HMS ''Birnbeck''" by the [[British Admiralty|Admiralty]] as part of the [[Department of Miscellaneous Weapons Development]] (DMWD) for research into new weapons.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Johnson|first1=Ted|title=Weston Super Mare & The Aeroplane|date=2013|publisher=Amberley Publishing|isbn=978-1445632148|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TJOIAwAAQBAJ&q=Admiralty+st+thomas+head&pg=PA1988-IA88}}</ref> To support this buildings were constructed at St Thomas Head, east of Middle Hope. Some of these have since been removed and the site is now used by [[QinetiQ]] as an explosives and shock test facility.<ref>{{PastScape|desc=St Thomas Head Weapons Testing Site|num=1460835|access-date=31 August 2015}}</ref>
